NL is a passively acquired autoimmune condition in newborns caused by the transplacental transfer of maternal autoantibodies—mainly anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB, and less commonly anti-U1 RNP—crossing the placenta (usually after 12–16 weeks of gestation); it is not true SLE in the baby.

Sjögren’s syndrome is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by dry eyes (xeropthalmia) and dry mouth (xerostomia), resulting from lymphocytic destruction of the salivary and lacrimal glands. It may occur as a primary condition (primary Sjögren’s syndrome) or in association with other autoimmune diseases such as RA and SLE, viral infections such as HIV and Epstein– Barr virus, and primary biliary cirrhosis (secondary Sjögren’s syndrome).

Dermatomyositis (DM) and polymyositis (PM) are inflammatory myopathies causing proximal muscle weakness. DM is marked by distinctive skin rashes (e.g., Gottron’s papules, heliotrope rash), whereas PM lacks skin involvement. Both may lead to significant functional impairment.
